result.summary: Pausanias continues describing Polygnotus' painting of the underworld at Delphi. He covers the daughters of Pandareus, Greek heroes such as Antilochus, Agamemnon, Achilles and Patroclus, the story of Phocus and Iaseus, and then Orpheus with the musicians Thamyris, Marsyas and Olympus.

scenes.title: Daughters of Pandareus
scenes.summary: Pausanias recounts Homer's tale of the orphaned daughters of Pandareus, snatched by the Harpies and given to the Furies, and describes their painted figures.
scenes.stakes: The orphaned girls are carried off by Harpies and given to the Furies.

scenes.title: Greek Heroes in the Painting
scenes.summary: Antilochus, Agamemnon, Protesilaus, Achilles and Patroclus are described in their poses; only Agamemnon is bearded.

scenes.title: Phocus, Iaseus, Maera, Actaeon
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains the signet-ring scene of Phocus and Iaseus, then describes Maera and Actaeon with his mother.
scenes.stakes: Phocus is later killed through Peleus' scheming.

scenes.title: Orpheus and the Musicians
scenes.summary: Orpheus sits in the willow grove with Promedon, Schedius, Pelias, Thamyris, Marsyas and Olympus; Pausanias adds the Phrygian tradition about Marsyas.
scenes.stakes: Thamyris is blind and dejected, his lyre broken.

analysis.text: The painting gathers figures of fate and loss, such as orphans, early deaths and failed musicians, fitting the underworld setting.
Pausanias reads the painting through Homer, the epic cycle and local traditions, showing how Greeks used art to preserve myth.

fun_facts.text: Polygnotus' Delphi paintings were in the Lesche of the Cnidians; Pausanias is our main source for them.

language_notes.text: The Harpies are storm-spirits who snatch people away; here they hand the girls to the Furies, avenging goddesses, as a kind of punishment for their parents' guilt.
Tantalus and Pandareus were both said to have stolen a golden dog of Zeus from Crete and then sworn falsely that they never had it.
Peleus and Telamon killed their half-brother Phocus out of jealousy; Pausanias mentions only Peleus' contrivance, assuming the story is known.
The Return from Ilium is a lost epic (Nostoi) about the Greek heroes' homecomings from Troy.
Actaeon was devoured by his own hounds after offending Artemis; the hound and fawn point to his hunting life and death.
Homer's Odyssey describes Proserpine's grove at the entrance to the underworld, with tall poplars and willows that shed their fruit.
Marsyas was a satyr who challenged Apollo at music and was flayed; the Phrygians identified him with a local river at Celaenae.

context_notes.text: Polygnotus was a famed Thasian painter; this is his great underworld painting (Nekyia) in the Cnidian clubhouse (Lesche) at Delphi.
Thamyris was a Thracian bard who boasted he could beat the Muses; they blinded him and took away his gift of song.
Celaenae was a Phrygian city; Cybele was the Asian mother goddess, and the Galati are the Gauls who invaded Asia Minor in the third century BC.

literary_notes.text: Beardlessness marks the young heroes while Agamemnon's beard marks his age and authority, so the painter distinguishes the figures visually.
The hound and fawn stand for Actaeon's hunting and his death by his own dogs, compressing his story into emblems.
Thamyris's broken lyre and torn strings symbolize the loss of his musical gift as punishment for his pride.
